The ionic conductivity, σ, can be linked to Dr according to the Nernst-Einstein equation, σ ¼ nq2DrHR kBT ; ð4Þ where n is carrier concentration with charge q and can be represented as n ¼ Ncð1  cÞ; ð5Þ where N is the concentration of energetically equivalent mobile-ion sites, and c is the fraction of mobile-ion sites occupied64. The conductivity equation becomes σ ¼ HRq2a2Ncð1  cÞν0 expðΔSm kB Þ bkBT exp  ΔHm kBT   : ð6Þ where ΔSm is the activation entropy, and ΔHm is the activation enthalpy (alsocalledtheactivationenergyoractivationbarrieranddenoted Ea).Theσ comprises two key factors, the exponential and pre-exponential terms. The pre-exponential component encompasses multiple factors, including the exponential dependence of entropy. Even a slight alteration in these factors, particularly within the exponential part, can substantially impact ion conduction. Consequently, this phenomenon explains why materials with similar structures do not necessarily exhibit similar ionic conductivity. Such complexities in understanding and generalizing materials’ behaviors pose signiﬁcant challenges. Anionic rotation Anion rotation is a phenomenon that occurs in some ionic compounds, where the anions can rotate around their axes, resulting in reorientation. It can be a partial or full rotation, depending on the materials and T. This can affect the ionic conductivity of the material, as the rotation can create or disrupt pathways for the migration of ions. This behavior makes the material unique and attractive. The anionic reorientational motion is directly identiﬁed by calculating the angular autocorrelation function (ζ) of anions65: ζðt0Þ ¼ 1 Ne X Ne j¼1 ^rjðt þ t0Þ  ^rjðtÞ * + t ð7Þ where ^rjðtÞ, and ^rjðt þ t0Þ denote the unit vectors connecting from the center of mass of anions to an edge atom in the same anion at time t and t þ t0, respectively. Ne is the number of edge atoms in the anion. This function typically shows an exponential decay (≈eλt0) within a short time witha decayrate λ.The anionreorientationalactivationenergy(Er a) also can be calculated using the Arrhenius equation: λ ¼ λ0 exp Er a kBT   ð8Þ where λ0 is the pre-exponential factor. It is important to emphasize that Er a (the activation energy for anions) and Ea (the activation energy for mobile ions) are two distinct quantities. Major classes of fast ion conductors The translationally immobile framework anion plays a huge role in cationic conduction. Therefore, we classiﬁed the fast ion conductors based on their framework structures: layered oxide materials, polyhedral connecting fra- mework materials, and cluster anion-type materials. Each class is unique, and they have a distinct role in cation conduction. Layered oxide materials Layered oxide materials are a class of solid fast ion conductors that have a distinctive structure consisting of mobile cations sandwiched between rigid frameworklayers.Thesematerialsexhibithighionicconductivity,especially for alkali metal ions, and have potential applications in electrochemical devices. Two importantsub-classesoflayeredoxide materialsareβ-alumina and honeycomb layered oxide. β-alumina. In the middle of thetwentieth century, a remarkable scientiﬁc advancement emerged in the ﬁeld of SFICs with the groundbreaking discovery of β-alumina by Yao and Kummer30. One of the most striking features of β-alumina is its impressive Ag+ ion conductivity (3.5 × 10−2 S cm−166 at 25 ∘C), which rivals conventional liquid electro- lytes. This level of conductivity is exceptional and has attracted signiﬁcant attention from researchers in the ﬁeld of solid-state ionics. Notably, β- alumina also demonstrates fast ion conduction for divalent and even trivalent cation67. This characteristic expands its potential applications and highlights its versatility as a solid-state ionic conductor. The ability of β-alumina to facilitate the rapid conduction of alkali metal ions is attributed to its unique crystal structure. This structure comprises interconnected channels or tunnels that enable the efﬁcient movement of ions, enhancing their conductivity. Since the discovery of β-alumina, extensive experimental68–71 and theoretical67,72–75 research efforts have been dedicated to gaining deeper insights into its ion transport properties and stability. Moreover, synthe- sizing these materials is straightforward, allowing researchers to obtain high-quality samples for study and characterization. The general formula of β-alumina is M2O.xAl2O3 (where M = Li, Na, Ag, K, and Rb)30. This materialconsistsoftwodistinctsubgroups:β0 andβ″,eachcharacterizedbya unique structure (Fig. 3a, e). The β″ type exhibits higher ionic conductivity due to its distinctive framework structure, accommodating a larger number of vacant cationic sites. The crystal structure of β-alumina comprises compact layers of spinel blocks formed by Al3+ tetrahedra and octahedra coordinated with oxygens. These spinel blocks are sandwiched between mobile cations, with oxygen bridges connecting them to form a 3D hex- agonal structure. In the case of β0-alumina, the space group is P63/mcm, while for β″-alumina, it is R3m. The layer between the rigid spinel blocks is often called the conduction layer (Fig. 3a, e). Within the conduction layer, three different cationic sites exist: anti-Beevers-Ross (aBR), Beevers-Ross (BR), and mid-Oxygen (mO) (Fig. 3d)68. The sites are different based on the local oxygen environment, such as BR is formed by three top and three bottom oxygens, and aBR is formed by two oxygens (one top and one bottom).Thesesitesare crucialinfacilitatingcationicdiffusionand hopping within the material, as presented in Fig. 3b. Occupancy at these sites and the diffusion mechanism have been subjects of intense debate and investigation76–78. Kummer conducted systematic experimental studies on various monovalent counterparts (Li+, Na+, Ag+, K+, Rb+) of β-alumina79. The studies revealed that the ionic radius, particularly between Na+ and Ag+, was suitable for ion diffusion within the β-alumina framework (Fig. 3c). This observation suggests the existence of an optimal cation size that maximizes diffusion within the material. MD studies by Wolf, Walker, and Catlow80 provided structural and dynamical properties of β″-alumina using inter-atomic potential parameters suggested by Walker and Catlow81. These MD simulations revealed the importance of non-stoichiometric composition in enhancing cationic dif- fusion and observed a transition from low-temperature hopping transport to a higher-temperature liquid-like transport80. Further MD studies by Thomas and Zendejas82 focused on Na-β″-alumina and provided additional atomistic insights into the diffusion of Na+ ions, including correlation effects and the presence of mobile and immobile Na+ ions in the diffusion mechanism. The conduction mechanisms in β0-alumina and β″-alumina differ. In β0-alumina, the dominant conduction mechanism involves the migration of oxygen ions (O2−) through the crystal lattice, utilizing oxygen vacancies as diffusion paths. In β″-alumina, the conduction mechanism revolves around the migration of sodium ions (Na+) through the crystal lattice, facilitated by https://doi.org/10.1038/s43246-024-00550-z Review article Communications Materials | (2024) 5:122
the presence of oxygen vacancies. In addition tothe oxygen, repulsive forces between Na ions were found to play a crucial role in reducing the activation energy required for ion diffusion, as observed by Sato and Kikuchi83 and further emphasized by Wang and Pickett84. Accurate description of lattice vibration was executed by ref. 85. They developedasetofpotentialparametersbyﬁttingphononvibrationalmodes, providing a accurate representation of lattice vibrations in Ag β-alumina. Their studies showed that mobile Ag+ ions in the conducting plane are distributed over BR and aBR sites, exhibiting asymmetric large thermal amplitudes. The repulsion between Ag ions inﬂuences the dynamics, transitioning the diffusion mechanism from random hopping to coopera- tive motion. Honeycomb layered oxides. Honeycomb Layered oxide solids have attracted considerable attention as potential electrode for sodium-ion batteries since NaxCoO2 was ﬁrst introduced as a cathode material86. However, the cation diffusion mechanism is similar to the other elec- trolytes. Typical layered honeycomb oxides consist of alkali or coinage metal atoms sandwiched between slabs made exclusively of transition metal and chalcogen (or pnictogen) atoms arranged in edge-shared octahedra in a honeycomb fashion (Fig. 3f). These materials offer several advantages, such as wider interstitial spaces between two-dimensional polyhedral framework layers that facilitate cation migration, enabling high ionic conductivity at RT, and excellent chemical and ambient stability87. Meanwhile, a rigid octahedral framework layer completely hinders diffusion along the crystalline c-direction. The materials are classiﬁed based on the local cationic environment, with oxygen (tetra- hedral, octahedral, or prismatic) sharing rectangular faces, thereby creating a wide BN for facile cation transport88. These layered honeycomb oxide structures differ from the β-alumina structure, where oxygen atoms are located in the conduction layer. Van der Waals forces weakly connect the framework layers in these honeycomb oxides, and the inter-layer distance can be adjusted by framework modiﬁcations or a larger size cationic substitution. Alkali ion conductivity is signiﬁcantly inﬂuenced by the inter-slab distance, cationic concentration, and their different octahedral arrangements in the framework layer. Several experimental and theoretical studies, including MD simula- tions and topological analysis, have been conducted to gain insights into alkaline ion conduction and material stability mechanisms88–90. Evstigneeva et al. synthesized a series of honeycomb layered materials, Na2M2TeO6 (where M = Ni, Zn, Mg, and Co), and discovered surprisingly high ionic conductivity88. The materials containing nickel (Ni) are well-suited for utilization as cathode materials, whereas materials substituted with zinc (Zn) and magnesium (Mg), offering a low electronic conductivity, are particularly suitable for serving as electrolytes, demonstrating noteworthy Na+ ion conductivities of 5.7 × 10−4 S cm−1 and 2.3 × 10−4 S cm−1 at RT, respectively91,92. Further investigations, focusing on the impact of homo- valent calcium ion (Ca2+) substitution and heterovalent gallium ion (Ga3+) substitution at the zinc (Zn) site within the Na2Zn2TeO6 structure, unveiled augmented ionic conductivities, measuring 7.5 × 10−4 S cm−1 and 1.1 × 10−3 S cm−1 at RT, respectively93,94. These ﬁndings indicate a pro- gression towards the superionic regime, deﬁned by ionic conductivities exceeding 1.0 × 10−3 S cm−1. Despite several improvements in materials synthesis, the funda- mental understanding was lacking. Taking a broader perspective, MD simulations of Na2Ni2TeO6 aim to understand the mechanism of sodium ion transport in honeycomb layered oxide materials. Sau and Kumar89 proposed interatomic potential for performing force-ﬁeld-based MD simulations on the series of honeycomb layered oxides (Na2M2TeO6). The force ﬁeld accurately reproduced the structural and dynamical properties observed experimentally. The MD studies revealed detailed cationic diffusion pathways, energy barriers along the diffusion path (Fig. 3f), and cationic migration mechanisms. The crystal structure of Na2Ni2TeO6 consists of three distinct cationic sites: 6g, 4c, and 2a, which are located at the center of trigonal bi-prisms formed by face- or edge- sharing NiO6 or TeO6 octahedra. The 2a site is energetically less favor- able due to the strong electrostatic repulsion between the Na+ ion and the Te6+ ion in the adjacent TeO6 octahedra. MD simulations revealed that the Na+ ions preferentially occupy the 6g and 4c sites, in agreement with the experimental ﬁndings of ref. 95. The 2a site becomes accessible only at temperatures above 500 K, but no phase transition has been reported at such high temperatures. The MD simulations also indicated that the 4c site is the most stable site for the Na+ ions; the number of 4c sites is equal to the number of Na+ ions, implying that some Na+ ions have to occupy the slightly higher energy 6g sites for avoiding a strongly correlated diffusion. Therefore, the most probable diffusion pathway for the Na+ ions is 4c-6g-4c89. The presence of Na+ ions in the higher energy sites suggests a cooperative mechanism of Na+ ion migration. The conductivity can be tuned by varying the cationic concentrations among the inter-layer on the conduction layer, as shown in Fig. 3g96, where there is a scope for studying concerted motion and their role in hopping energy barrier. A general characteristic of honeycomb layered material can be deﬁned in a radar plot, as shown in Fig. 3h. Sau et al. expanded their MD study to several other honeycomb layered oxide materials, such as A2Ni2TeO6 97, where A = Li, Na, and K, and Na2LiFeTeO6 98. Figure 3j indicates the goodness of the structural ﬁtting with the XRD structure, whereas a comparative study in A2Ni2TeO6 for different cation sizes can provide insights into how different factors, such as ion–ion repulsion99, pressure, temperature, and structural stability, affect the diffusion, con- ductivity, and occupancy of cations at different cationic sites. The study revealed an exponential relationship between cationic diffusion, inter-layer distances (Fig. 3k), inverse relationship with activation energy (Fig. 3l), and different cationic occupancy patterns with increasing cationic sizes63. Notably, a ring-type diffusion mechanism was found in Na2LiFeTeO6, similar to other classes of materials like garnet100. This ring-type diffusion is also known as a billiard-ball mechanism101. Later, Masese et al. made signiﬁcant contributions to the domain of high-voltage battery applications by identifying and reporting several pro- mising materials102,103. Conventionally, materials in this category are char- acterized by a single conduction layer. However, their work has yielded a particularly intriguing material, namely Ag6M2TeO6 (where M can repre- sent Ni, Mg, or other transition metal atoms), which exhibits a distinctive structure featuring bi-layers of Ag atoms within Ag-rich crystalline domains, as depicted in Fig. 3i90. This bi-layer-type honeycomb layered oxide conﬁguration represents a unique and novel structural motif. In order to explore the distinctive properties of these bilayer-type honeycomb layered oxides, a preliminary MD simulation was conducted using a previously reported force ﬁeld, with interaction parameters similar to those of Na2Ni2TeO6. During this simulation, the polyhedral layers were held ﬁxed at their centers to prevent any bending. Interestingly, the theo- retical simulation successfully conﬁrmed the formation of these bilayer structures using the predeﬁned force ﬁeld. In the case of Ag6M2TeO6, it was observed that the inter-layer distance is relatively substantial, approximately 6 Å, in contrast to Na2Ni2TeO6, which exhibits an inter-layer distance of approximately 3 Å. Consequently, mobile cations within the bilayer tend to approach the oxygen layer, resulting in a splitting of the Ag+ conduction layer. However, it is essential to emphasize that a more comprehensive and detailed investigation is needed to gain a thorough understanding of the cationicdiffusionalpathwaysand theunderlyingdiffusionmechanismsthat govern these intriguing materials. Key challenges and prospects. These materials face several obstacles, including but not limited to low ionic conductivity under ambient con- ditions, restricted diffusion along the c-direction owing to non- penetrable rigid framework layers, structural instability stemming from larger inter-layer separations, and volumetric alterations during ion migration. Conversely, a weakly connecting framework affords facile adjustments of the inter-layer spacing, a parameter that exhibits expo- nential dependence on ionic diffusion. Additionally, the doubled-layered honeycomb oxides represent a relatively new area. https://doi.org/10.1038/s43246-024-00550-z Review article Communications Materials | (2024) 5:122
Polyhedral connecting framework materials Polyhedral Connecting Framework Materials is another class that exhibits a 3D network of polyhedra. These polyhedra, which can be of various shapes, such as tetrahedra and octahedra, are connected at their corners or edges to form a continuous framework. This structure creates channels or cages where mobile ions can reside. The connectivity and geometry of the poly- hedra can greatly inﬂuence the material’s properties, including its thermal stability, electronic structure, and ion conductivity. The important sub- classes of these materials are Lithium Garnet, LGPS-type, Thio-/LISICONs, and NASICONs. Lithium garnet. This type of materials, with the general chemical formula A3B2(XO4)3 (A = Ca, Mg, Y, La or rare earth; B = Al, Fe, Ga, Ge, Mn, Ni or V; X = Si, Ge, Al), promise high thermal stability, wide electrochemical Fig. 3 | Characteristics of layered oxide materials (polyhedral models), diffusion paths, and structural differences. a Polyhedral model representing β0-alumina. b Visualization of the Na+ ion path within the conduction plane67. c Different cationic species and their diffusion coefﬁcient and activation energies, Ea 30. d Depiction of various cationic sites within the conduction plane68. e Polyhedral model depicting β″-alumina, highlighting structural differences and distinct cationic diffusion mechanisms compared to β0-alumina. f Polyhedral models showcasing single-layered honeycomb oxides, including mean cationic distribution and mean energy on the conducting layer. The cationic distribution and mean energy ﬁgures are reproduced from ref. 63, copyright (Elsevier, 2022). g Relationship between cationic concentration at the conduction plane and cationic conductivity96. h A radar plot depicting a general characteristic of honeycomb-layered oxides. i Polyhedral models illustrating double-layered honeycomb oxides90. j Distribution of framework atoms at the ab-plane obtained from MD simulation, with crystallographic locations marked for comparison98. k, l Exponential dependency of cationic behavior with inter-layer distances, d, along with trends in the inter-layer distance and activation energy of cation, Ea, for different cations based on experimental and MD simulation data63. https://doi.org/10.1038/s43246-024-00550-z Review article Communications Materials | (2024) 5:122
window, as well as high ionic conductivity104. They generally stabilize in the cubic phase with the space group Ia3d. The A, B, and X sites are, respectively, 8-fold (anti-prismatic), 6-fold (octahedral), and fourfold (tetrahedral) coordinated to oxygen (Fig. 4a). Lithium conducting garnets, Li3Ln3Te2O12 (Ln = Y, Pr, Nd, Sm-Lu), typically contain 5–7 formula units in a unit cell where lithium ions occupy tetrahedral and octahedral sites, as depicted in Fig. 4b. Since the original work by ref. 104, it has attracted numerous experimental and theoretical studies. It is observed that at low lithium content, Li3Ln3Te2O12, where Li+ ions are tetrahedrally coordinated, does not show signiﬁcant ionic conductivity (Fig. 4c)23,105. Whereas, higher ionic conductivity has been achieved for Li-rich, “stuffed garnets,” such as Li5La3M2O12 (M = Nb, Ta, and Sb), Li6ALa2M2O12 (A = Mg, Ca, Sr, and Ba; M = Nb and Ta), and Li7La3M2O12 (M = Zr and Sn)106 where Li ions occupy the tetrahedral as well as octahedral interstitial sites partially, increasing migrational entropy, ΔSm (Eq. (6)). Generally, the conductivity increases with higher Li content. It is enhanced by two to three orders of magnitude from Li3Ln3Te2O12 to Li7La3M2O12 due to signiﬁcant Li+ occupancy, which switches from tetrahedral to octahedral sites23,105. One of the most widely studied compositions of the lithium garnet series is Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO). This high-conducting cubic garnet was reported by ref. 104, and later on, the tetragonal phase was detected at a lower temperature by ref. 107. The cubic phase exhibits two orders of magnitude higher conductivity than the tetragonal phase108. Several com- putational studies have been conducted to explain such behavior109,110. The low-temperature tetragonal phase exhibits synchronous collective Li+ ion hopping, causing a high activation energy barrier. In cubic LLZO, the Li+ ﬁnds unoccupied sites, resulting in uncorrelated Li+ motion that costs less activation energy100. In contrast, a few ab initio MD studies by refs. 111,45 identiﬁed the concerted motion of Li+ ions (two or three Li+ ions jump together). Therefore, the Li+ ion diffusion mechanism is still under debate. Hu et al.112, and others113–115 reported that higher valent ion (Al3+) sub- stitution at Li sublattice improves the stability of cubic garnet of nominal composition in Li7La3Zr2O12. The Al3+ substitution generates more Li sites, leading to higher conﬁgurational entropy and reducing the free energy barrier between two Li+ ion hops. Furthermore, the aliovalent substitutions (e.g., Ta5+) at Zr sites also enhance the ionic conductivity116,117. An order of magnitude conductivity is enhanced from Li5La3Ta2O12 to Li6BaLa2Ta2O12 116,118,119 where the Li ions are occupied in tetrahedral as well as octahedral sites118,120. Thus, garnet-type materials are found to be pro- misingfastionconductorsowingtotheirwiderangeofsubstitutionsandthe stability of their skeleton structure. LGPS-type. In 2011, ref. 6 reported a unique 3D framework structure (Li10GeP2S12) known as an LGPS-type structure, which exhibited a remarkable order of magnitude higher lithium-ion conductivity (12 mS cm−1 at ambient temperature) than the best Li+ ion conductivity reported in last decades among the sulﬁdes. This discovery represented a signiﬁcant breakthrough in solid-state fast ion conductors and prompted further exploration of these materials for application in ASSBs. The LGPS-type material has a general formula of Li4−xGe1−xPxS4, where x = 2/3. The crystal structure can be described as a tetragonal cell with space group P42/nmc. The framework structure consists of (Ge0.5P0.5)S4, PS4, and LiS4-tetrahedra, forming a complex network. The (Ge0.5P0.5)S4 tetrahedra and LiS6 octahedra are connected by edge-sharing, forming a one-dimensional (1D) chain along the c-direction, further inter- connected by PS4 tetrahedra. The lithium-ion channel comprises 16h, 4d, 4c, and 8f sites, although the existence of the 4c site remains a subject of debate. The origin of the high ionic conduction exhibited by LGPS-type materials has been extensively investigated through theoretical studies. MD simulations suggest that the high conductivity may arise from col- lective ion migrations along the 1D path facilitated by Coulombic interactions among the lithium ions. This phenomenon, known as the cooperative migration mechanism, involves the coordination and movement of multiple Li+ ions within the available conduction pathways, resulting in enhanced ionic conductivity. Even though LGPS-type structures exhibit high Li+ ion conductivity, a portion of Li+ ions remains localized at octahedral sites, not contributing to Li+ ion diffusion. This material exhibits highly anisotropic Li+ conduction through partially occupied tetrahedral Li-sites with a low activation energy of 0.24 eV. However, the atomic origins of these characteristics remained unclear until Mo et al. shed light on the topic by conducting ab initio MD simulations, supporting the hypothesis of Li+ ion diffusion along the c- direction59. Adams and Rao109 performed MD simulations based on force ﬁelds to gain deeper insights, revealing the atomistic dynamics of Li ions. They found that Li+ ions are distributed along the c-direction among several interstitial Li sites. The study also indicated the possibility of PS4 3/GeS4 2− rotation, which facilitates Li+ ion dynamics through a paddle-wheel mechanism121. To replace the expensive germanium (Ge) component, ref.122synthesized Li10SnP2S12,which gained considerable attentiondue to its comparable ionic conductivity to liquids or polymers, negligible elec- tronic conductivity, and cost-effectiveness. A recently developed material, Li11Si2PS12 (LGPS-type material) by ref. 123, exhibited higher conductivity than LGPS at RT with an activation energy of ~0.19 eV. Subsequently, ref. 2 synthesized materials such as Li9.54Si1.74P1.44S11.7Cl0.3 with an ionic con- ductivity of 25 mS cm−1 at RT, posing a similar structure as LGPS. Another study by ref. 124 investigated Na11Sn2PnX12 (Pn = P, Sb; X = S, Se) and found that framework tetrahedral rotation (PnX3 4 ) introduced dynamic frustration in the energy landscape of Na11Sn2PS12 and Na11Sn2PSe12, enabling facile sodium (Na) ion diffusion. For a conductivity comparison, an Arrhenius plot is displayed in Fig. 4f. In SFICs, introducing halogen is pivotal in transforming the ion dif- fusion mechanism from 1D to 3D at ambient temperature. This phenom- enon is attributed to the ability of halogens to diminish the interaction between the framework anion and the migrating ions, thereby facilitating facile ion transport. In the silicon-based system, Li9.54Si1.74P1.44S11.7Cl0.3 crystal structure exempliﬁes the transformative effect of halogen incor- poration. As depicted in Fig. 4d, the unit cell comprises 1D polyhedral chains interconnected by PX4 (X = Cl, Br, I) tetrahedra, providing a network of interconnected pathways (Fig. 4e) for Li+ ion migration. The Li+ ions occupy the 16h, 8f, and 4c interstitial sites. This material is the ﬁrst to exhibit awidelydispersed3DdiffusionchannelwithintheLGPS-typeframeworkat ambient temperature, leading to an exceptionally high ionic conductivity of 25 mS cm−1 at RT. Thio-/LISICONs. Signiﬁcant research efforts have been dedicated to enhancing the ionic conductivity in Lithium Super Ionic Conductors (LISICONs). In 1978, Hong identiﬁed poor ionic conductivity (10−7 S cm−1 at ambient temperature) in Li14Zn(GeO4)4 and related materials such as Li4GeO4-LiVO4, Li2+2xZn1−xGeO4, Li2O-V2O5-SiO2, and Li4SiO4-Li3PO4, which were synthesized around the same period and exhibited slightly improved ionic conductivity125–129. Replacing oxide ions (O2−) with sulﬁde ions (S2−) in the LISICON structure has signiﬁcantly enhanced cationic conductivity. This phenomenon can be attributed to the larger ionic radius and lower electronegativity of S2−compared to O2−, both of which favor high ionic conductivity. The general formula for thio- LISICONs is Li4xM1yM0 yS4S4, where M can be Si, Ge, or Sn; M0 can be P, Al, Zn, Ga, or Sb; and x and y are compositional parameters. Notable materials in this class include Li4GeS4, Li4SiS4, Li4SnS4, Li3PS4, and Li2ZrS3), and Li2ZrS3,all of which exhibit ionic conductivities in theorder of 10−5 S cm−1. The structural arrangement of thio-LISICONs differs from that of LGPS-type materials. In thio-LISICONs, Li+ ions and Ge atoms are located at the octahedral and tetrahedral sites, respectively, and S2−are arranged in a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) fashion (Fig. 4(g)), whereas in LGPS-type materials, the S2−are arranged in a body-centered cubic (bcc) position. Aliovalent doping can further enhance the Li+ ion conductivity of thio-LISICONs. For instance, in the case of homovalent substitutions in Li3PO4, replacing O with S reduces the activation energy for Li+ ion migration from 1.5 to 0.5 eV. Heterovalent substitutions can also signiﬁcantly reduce the activation energy; for example, partial replacement of P5+ by Ge4+ with adjusting Li+ ion in Li3PO4 reduces the https://doi.org/10.1038/s43246-024-00550-z Review article Communications Materials | (2024) 5:122
activation energy and enhances ionic conductivity (Li3.25Ge0.25P0.75O4 exhibits ionic conductivity of 2.2 mS cm−1 at RT in this class). The structure of Li4GeS4, a representative thio-LISICON material. This material exhibits an isolated linear chain along the b-axis, offering one directional diffusion path. NASICONs. After the discovery of β-alumina, there was a strong belief in existing similar types of materials with 3D ion conduction130. The expectation became a reality when refs. 31,44 synthesized NASICON (an acronym for Na SuperIonic CONductor), marking a pivotal break- through. NASICON exhibits promising characteristics, including high 3D ionic conductivity, low thermal expansion, as well as high chemical stability. It is a class of 3D materials with remarkable RT ionic con- ductivity (≈10−3 S cm−1131). Furthermore, NASICONs offer adaptability through a wide range of substitutional windows, providing potential for further improvement. The general formula for NASICON is AMM0P3O12, where “A” can be monovalent or divalent alkaline earth ions. The M and M0 sites are occupied by di- (Zn2+, Cd2+,Ni2+, Mn2+, Co2+), tri- (Fe3+, Sc3+, Ti3+, V3+, Cr3+, Al3+, In3+, Ga3+, Y3+, Lu3+), tetra- (Ti4+, Zr4+, Hf4+, Sn4+,Si4+, Ge4+), and penta- (V5+,Nb5+,Ta5+, Sb5+, As5+) valent atoms132. A representative structure of Li-substituted NASICON (LiTi2(PO4)3) is displayed in Fig. 5a. The material consists of a framework structure built from corner-sharing tetrahedra and octahedra, forming a rhombohedral unit cell with R3c symmetry. The basic unit of the fra- mework consists of two TiO6-octahedra and three PO4-tetrahedra. These units, in turn, are connected to form “ribbons” along the c-axis, and the ribbons are joined together along the a- and b- by PO4-tetrahedra. In Li- counter part of NASICONs, 6b, 18e, and 36f Wyckoff sites were identiﬁed along the Li+ conduction channel. Complex hydrides. In SFIC, the comparison between β-alumina and NASICONs has been a subject of scientiﬁc exploration. However, it was not until 2007 that hydride materials, which have been studied for hydrogen storage, were recognized for their potential as fast ion conductors156. A pivotal discovery was made when it was found that Li+ ions exhibited signiﬁcant conduction behavior in LiBH4 after a structural transition from orthorhombic to hexagonal at 380 K with an approximate conductivity of 10−3 S cm−1157–159. This breakthrough propelled the research focus towards hydrides and their derivatives as solid electrolytes for ASSBs, owing to their remarkable ionic conductivity, high thermal and chemical stability, lightweight nature, stability against metal anode, and favorable mechanical properties, making them an ideal interface between the electrode and electrolyte. In light of the promising characteristics exhibited by hydrides, it is imperative to address several formidable challenges before realizing their practical utility, with a notable concern being their relatively deﬁcient ionic conductivity at RT157. Taking lithium borohydride (LiBH4) as an illustrative example, it is evident that its RT ionic conductivity is signiﬁcantly limited, being three to four orders of magnitude lower than desired157. However, a phase transition occurs at elevated temperatures, speciﬁcally at 388 K, leading to a remarkable augmentation in lithium-ion mobility, culminating in an impressive conductivity value of 5 × 10−3 S cm−1 at 423 K156,158–160. This underscores the pivotal role played by phase transitions within this class of materials. Consequently, it is paramount to gain a comprehensive under- standing of the intricacies surrounding phase transition phenomena, encompassing the underlying factors and origins. This improved ionic conductivity in LiBH4 arises due to the rotational disorder of the [BH4]−units in the high-T phase, a unique characteristic of such materials. The cationic sites’ lattice disorder contributes to the high ionic conductivity, and the rotational disorder of BH4 units has been investigated through techniques such as synchrotron X-ray powder dif- fraction, QENS, and ab initio MD simulations161–164. Driven by the objective of achieving high ionic conductivity, various efforts have been dedicated to stabilizing the highly conductive phase at or near RT. One approach involves doping halides into LiBH4, resulting in compounds such as Li(BH4)1−x Xx (X = Cl, Br, and I), where an RT high conducting phase is observed for x > 0.25 (0 < 1), particularly in the case of iodine doping156. Another popular strategy involves incorporating neutral molecules, such as LiBH4⋅1/2NH3, which also exhibit notable ionic conductivity (σ(Li+) = 7 × 10−4 S cm−1 at 40 °C)165. A more in-depth discussion regarding the role of these neutral molecules will be presented subsequently in this section on materials. By tuning the size and shape of the anions and cations, one can manipulate the diffusion pathways and barriers for cationic diffusion. This leads to the formation of other complex hydrides, such as M2BnHn, where (M = Li, Na, and n = 10, 12), that have wider interstitial spaces and thus facilitate cation diffusion. In pursuit of developing efﬁcient solid electrolytes for advanced battery technologies, signiﬁcant research has been dedi- cated to thiophosphate-based materials. Among these, lithium argyr- odites have emerged as a highly researched class, with promising ionic conductive properties reaching up to 24 mS cm−1182. However, it is important to note that these materials often exhibit varying degrees of disorder, particularly in the form of anion exchange between halogens and sulfur sites. This anion exchange has a signiﬁcant inﬂuence on the cationic transport properties, prompting numerous studies aimed at understanding the impact of iso- and aliovalent substitutions on this exchange process. Nevertheless, altering the chemical composition introduces complexities in comprehending the resultant transport properties, thereby making it challenging to isolate individual inﬂuences. Arising from the general formula Li7PS6, argyrodites display a transi- tion from a normal to a superionic phase (orthorhombic to a cubic phase, featuring the space group F43m). Their RT ionic conductivity remains relativelylow, with valuesaround 1.6 × 10−6 S cm−1183. The high-conducting phase canbe stabilized byintroducingcompositionssuch asLi6PS5X (where X represents a halogen atom like Cl, Br, I, or a vacancy). In the cubic phase, Li+ ions occupy 24g and 48h sites, S atoms are found in 4a and 4c sites, P atoms are situated in 4b sites, and either halide atoms (X) or vacancies occupy 4a sites. Speciﬁcally, the S atoms at 4a sites form PS4 tetrahedra with P atoms at 4b sites, while the S atoms at 4c sites bridge between PS4 tetra- hedra (as depicted in Fig. 7a)184–188. The Li ions are distributed in octahedral coordination around the S atoms. The presence of various interstitial sites surrounding the halide ions facilitates high ionic conductivity (Fig. 7c), typically within the range of 10−2–10−3 S cm−1 at RT, with low activation energies typically around 0.2 to 0.3 eV189. Among the single halide argyrodites, Li6PS5Cl exhibits the highest ionic conductivity at ambient temperature, ~10−3 S cm−1, followed by Li6PS5Br with around 10−4 S cm−1, while Li6PS5I displays the lowest ionic conductivity, ~10−6 S cm−1, as illustrated in Fig. 7b. General understanding and common features The development of solid ion conductors has primarily relied on the ion conduction mechanism described by Eq. (6), where ion movement occurs through hopping within a crystalline lattice11,211. Many structural families have demonstrated reasonably high Li-ion conductivity at RT, with the ability to vary Li-ion conductivity by several orders of magnitude within the same crystal framework structures10,211. Therefore, this section is dedicated to understanding the common and unique characteristics of the fast ion- conducting materials examined in this review. Coordination number Early studies found that the conditions in which the high ionic conductivity is realized with monovalent cation in a four- (tetrahedral) and three- coordinated conﬁgurations with the anions212. Recent studies have expan- ded this idea to link the high ionic conductivity observed in lithium sulﬁdes (e.g., LGPS and Li7P3S11) to bcc sulfur-sublattice, which can lead to energetically-equivalent tetrahedral (four-coordinated) sites of lithium and large transport channels11. Collective motion Several studies revealed that the collective (or cooperative) transport of lithium ions can ﬂatten the migration energy barrier, thereby facilitating rapid ion conduction in materials like LGPS, cubic LLZO, and NASICONs152,213,214.Inthesematerials,ithasbeenobserved that,onaverage, two to three Li-ions migrate simultaneously45,111,215. For instance, Burbano et al.100 identiﬁed the presence of string-like ion clusters that engage in cooperative motion within LLZO.Similarly, a ring-like mechanism was also reported in Na2LiFeTeO6 98. On the contrary, some studies reported that the strong cation-cation correlation is responsible for slow cation diffusion100. Hence, lower activation energy due to the collective diffusion of ions is subject to further investigation. Paddle-wheel effect Most recently, superionic conductors (such as Li3PS4, Li2B12H12, NaCB9H10, LiNaSO4, Na2SO4, Na3PO4, LiBH4, Li3SBF4, Na3SBCl4, etc.) containing anion clusters (i.e., PS4 3−, B12H12 2−, CB9H10 −, SO4 2−, PO4 3−, BH4 −, BF4 −, BCl4 −, etc.) have become a fertile group to search for high ionic conductivity175,177,180,216,217. An interesting feature of these ionic conductors is the so-called paddle-wheel effect characterized by a strong correlation between the translational motion of the cation and the rotational motion of anion cluster216, as depicted in Fig. 8(c), where the anionic rotation triggers the cationic diffusion. Under thermal excitation, non-spherical clusters can lead to a rotationally disordered phase, creating low-energy pathways for ionic migrations and greatly enhancing ionic conductivity175,217–219. This is exempliﬁed by the high Na-ion conductivity of 30 mS cm−1 of NaCB9H10 as it enters a rotationally disordered phase at RT. Kweon et al.175 supported the paddle-wheel behavior in A2B12H12 (A = Li and Na) by overlapping the translational diffusion frequency of cation and rotational frequency of anion. Therefore, fully exploiting the rotational degrees of freedom and utilizing the paddle-wheel effect could be a viable way to achieve high cation conductions. Most of the known cluster-containing ionic conductors exhibit a transition to the rotational disordered phase at high temperatures (higher than RT)167,172,220. It has been found that an amorphous structure with low density and a relatively large volume to accommodate the cluster cansupportthepaddle-wheeleffectevenatlowtemperatures(e.g.,RT)216,221. Such as in the case of Li2SO4, and α-Na3PO4 222, the polyanion rotation unexpectedly reduces the cationic conduction. On the other hand, ref. 223 argued that the doping of BH4 in Li-argyrodite enhanced the Li+-ion con- duction, which originated from weak interaction between Li and BH4 instead of the anion rotational effect. Therefore, the high cationic conduc- tion driven by the anion rotational effect is under a long debate. Introducing anharmonicity Anharmonicity is the deviation of a system from being a harmonic oscil- lator, which means that the restoring force is not proportional to the dis- placement of the system (Fig. 8f). Anharmonicity plays an important role in ion conduction. Several theoretical and experimental studies (DFT calcu- lations and neutron scattering experiments) have been performed recently to understand the phonon modes that are coupled most strongly with ionic conductivity and assess the role of anharmonicity. It has been ascertained that the anharmonicity inherent in the phonon vibrational modes of the host lattice exhibits substantial coupling with cationic diffusion. This phe- nomenon has been notably observed in AgI224. The recognized strong coupling between mobile ions and the host lattice holds pivotal importance for the diffusion process. Furthermore, investigations extended to materials like AgCrSe2, CuCrSe2, Li7P3S11, Li10GeP2S12, β-Li3PS4, Li3YBr6, and Li3ErCl6 have revealed analogous coupling phenomena (refs. 225,226). Dimensionality 3D diffusion pathways are crucial for achieving high ion conductivity, as they provide a lower possibility of blocking the ion conduction path. Structures that possess 3D diffusion pathways11 often exhibit a correlation with high ion conductivity, while lower dimensionalities227 often result in reduced ionic transport due to the potential obstruction of diffusion channels by defects228, even though the conductivity eq. (6) tells a different story, as the dimension term is in the denominator. Optimal bottleneck radius Ionic conductors with intrinsically low activation barriers are highly desirable. SFICs exhibit ionic conduction through polyhedral faces, leading to dynamic changes in the coordination environment of the migrating ion. These transitions create structural bottlenecks (BNs) within the diffusion pathway, directly inﬂuencing the activation energy barriers associated with ion migration229. Edge-sharing polyhedra typically present less favorable pathways for ion transport compared to face-sharing conﬁgurations. This is attributed to the generally smaller BNs, which encountered signiﬁcant changes in the coordination environment during ion jumps in edge-sharing structures230. Structural modiﬁcations arising from substitutions can frus- trate energy landscapes175,231,232, which impacts changing BNs radius233,234 (see Fig. 2a), consequently changing of the migration mechanism11,111. https://doi.org/10.1038/s43246-024-00550-z Review article Communications Materials | (2024) 5:122
Generally, substituting larger atoms into the polyhedral framework struc- ture results in a decrease in the activation barrier (see Fig. 5d) due to a widening of the diffusion bottleneck11,139). Of particular importance are materials possessing a percolating, 3D extended network composed of connected polyhedra with similar coordi- nation environments (widening BN radius). This structural characteristic can be achieved, for instance, by exclusively incorporating face-sharing polyhedra of the mobile species11. Such an arrangement minimizes the change in the coordination environment and naturally results in low acti- vation barriers. However, it is crucial to recognize that an excessively wide BN does not necessarily guarantee enhanced ion conduction134. In many cases, an optimal, moderate BN size proves efﬁcient ion transport, con- tingent upon the speciﬁc cation sizes and framework anion characteristics. Na-designing principles While Li-ion and Na-ion conductors share similar chemistry, their optimal design principles differ. Unlike Li-ion conductors, Na-ion conductors beneﬁt from face-sharing high-coordination number (CN) sites in their diffusion channels. This unique feature, proposed by ref. 46, is exempliﬁed by Na β-alumina and P2-type NaCoO2. Both materials possess face-sharing prismatic Na sites with large bottleneck sizes, enabling direct Na+ hopping with low energy barriers (0.26 eV in P2-type NaCoO2). This contrasts with structures lacking face-sharing, like O3-type NaMO2, which exhibit high energy barriers (0.76 eV) due to unfavorable intermediate sites. The face- sharing arrangement facilitates efﬁcient Na+ movement by avoiding these energy-intensive pathways. Therefore, in designing high-performance Na- ion conductors, incorporating face-sharing high-CN sites emerges as a critical strategy. This principle joins other established design elements like largeNa+ sites,3Ddiffusionnetworks,and astronginductiveeffect,offering a valuable tool for developing next-generation Na-ion battery materials. Another important factor is polyhedral rotation or tilting, that can further facilitate cation conduction (Fig. 9g), by introducing structural frustration, enabling a ﬂatter energy landscape. Recently, multiple linear regressions have become a valuable tool to understand the correlation of activation energy and other determining parameters for fast ion conduction (see Fig. 9i). Overall, the important parameters responsible for achieving ideal fast ion conduction are high- lighted in Fig. 9h.

For cations, (a) introducing disordered sites because of structural distortion can ﬂatten the energy landscape. b It can also make a uniform coordination environment. Uniform coordination numbers can offer a lower energy barrier for cationic hop- ping. c A three-dimensional ion-conducting channel is highly recommended for high ionic conduction. d A high concentration of mobile ions, and a vacancy-rich structure favors high ion conduction. e Multiple ion migration also favors fast ion conduction. f For anions, the ideal features encompass a highly frustrated structure, anion modiﬁcations generating new conduction sites, and (g) octahedral tilting (rotational anions) facilitating enhanced cationic diffusion through a paddle-wheel mechanism. These properties collectively contribute to efﬁcient and rapid ion conduction within the material. h Low activation energy, optimal bottleneck, opti- mal cationic vacancy, cation-cation correlation (can vary depending on the case), higher dimensional diffusion, moderate iso/aliovalent substitution, and polyhedral rotation are the keys to achieving high ion conduction. i Pattern detection employing multiple linear regression techniques (Ea = a1P1 + a2P2 + b, where Pi represents the selected properties, ai and b represent the ﬁtted parameters, the R2 is ﬁtting coefﬁ- cient) focusing on correlation analysis between activation energy (Ea) and other descriptors (Pi) such as electronegativity, distance between two anions (in the case of cluster type anion), etc. The diagonal terms represent the correlation with Ea vs. {Pi}, whereas the other terms represent Ea vs. {Pi, Pj}. & Shin-ichi Orimo 1,3 All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) are promising alternatives to conventional lithium-ion batteries. ASSBs consist of solid-fast-ion-conducting electrolytes and electrodes that offer improved energy density, battery safety, speciﬁc power, and fast-charging capability. Despite decades of intensive research, only a few have high ionic conductivity at ambient temperature. Developing fast ion- conducting materials requires both synthesis of high-conducting materials and a fundamental understanding of ion transport mechanisms. However, this is challenging due to wide variations of the ionic conductivity, even within the same class of materials, indicating the strong inﬂuence of structural modiﬁcations on ion transport. This Review discusses three selected material classes, namely layered oxides, polyhedral connections, and cluster anion types, as promising fast ion conductors. Emphasis is placed on the inherent challenges and the role of the framework structure on mobile ion conduction. We elucidate strategies to address these challenges by leveraging theoretical frameworks and insights from materials science. Solid fast-ion conductors represent a distinct class of ion-conducting materials characterized by the diffusion of a speciﬁc type of atom through the interstitial spaces within a solid lattice while other atoms remain translationally immobile at their crystal sites. This unique behavior allows liquid-like fast ion conduction of the particular atom within a solid fra- mework. Notably, solid fast-ion conductors (SFICs) exhibit comparable ionic conduction to the liquid electrolyte solution, particularly those in organic solvents1, such as 25 mS cm−1 for Li9.54Si1.74P1.44S11.7Cl0.3 2, and 70 mS cm−1 for Na2(CB9H10)(CB11H12)3 at room temperature (RT). Additionally, these materials have extended operating temperature range comparedtotheirliquidcounterparts4–8,higherenergydensitywhileusedin battery, longer life cycles, and enhanced safety due to the absence of organic liquid or polymer electrolytes9–12. The technological applications of SFIC are of signiﬁcant interest, particularly in the development of all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs), fuel cells, and gas sensors2,13,14. Recently, SFICs have also been a promising candidate in solid-state barocaloric cooling/heating applications15–17. ASSBs, in particular, are considered promising candidates for high-energy-density batteries, addressing the growing demand in the electric vehicle market as conventional lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) approach the theoretical limit9. Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs), another important application, can also beneﬁt from the utilization of SFICs. Operating at elevated temperatures, SOFCs require stable and efﬁcient materials to ensure optimal performance. Conducting ions in a solid phase faces various challenges due to the dense packing of atoms within the crystal structure, which limits the availability of space for ionic diffusion. As a result, the ionic conductivity in solids is generally low. The development of SFICs has witnessed notable progress18,19 in synthesizing new materials (Fig. 1a). Researchers have exploreda diverse range of mobile ionic species, including but not limitedto Li+, Na+, H+, Ag+, Cu+, F−, and H−to enhance the performance of SFICs. Recent reviews have extensively documented and summarized this progress4,20–25. In addition to materials that conduct monovalent ions, there is growing interest in the potential of divalent-cation-conducting materials, such as Mg2+, Ca2+, and Zn2+ for various energy-storage applications7,26,27. These materials garner attention due to their signiﬁcant promise in energy- storage devices, primarily attributed to their higher energy densities when compared to ASSBs constructed using monovalent cations. Remarkably, ions such as O2−and Mg2+ have demonstrated notable ionic conductivity, achieving an impressive value up to 0.1 mS cm−1 at RT7. Inorganic solid electrolytes can be classiﬁed into oxide, sulﬁde, halide, and hydride categories based on their chemistry33. Whereas, in this review, they are classiﬁed based on their framework anion structural connectivity, as displayed in Fig. 1b. Among oxide-based materials, Lithium Super Ionic Conductors (LISICONs), Na Super Ionic Conductors (NASICONs), garnets, perovskites, and anti- perovskites are the most widely studied34,35. In halide based materials, Li3MX6 (M = Y, Er; X = Cl, Br, I) Li2ZrCl6 36, and LaCl3 37 are found attractive, owing to the high ionic conductivity (≈1 mS cm−1 at room temperature) and a higher electro- chemical stability comparable to known oxides38,39 and sulﬁdes. Complex metal hydrides fall under the hydride category. Each group of materials has distinct advantages: oxide-based electrolytes generally exhibit lower ionic conductivity and high hardness but superior stability in atmospheric and electrode environments. Sulﬁde and hydride-based electrolytes, on the other hand, tend to demonstrate higher ionic conductivity, though they are quite sensitive to ambient conditions. Notably, the mixture of two complex hydrides (NaCB9H10 and NaCB11H12) has achieved the highest known ionic conductivity thus far, based on our current knowledge40. Here, we classiﬁed these materials into three major classes. Consequently, this review places particular emphasis on complex hydrides and mono-valent conducting ions as a topic of special interest. Fundamentals of ion conduction The ion conduction mechanisms in solid-state electrolytes differ sig- niﬁcantly from those in liquid electrolytes. In liquid electrolytes, the trans- port of ions involves their movement within the solvent medium. In contrast, in crystalline solids, the conduction of ions requires passing through periodic BN points, creating an energy barrier between two local energy minima. The Stokes-Einstein equation describesthe relationship between ion diffusion, solvent viscosity, ion size and temperature, indicating that lower solvent viscosity leads to higher ion mobility61. Fast molecule-ion exchange is necessary for fast ion conduction in liquid electrolytes. In contrast, in crystalline solids, the diffusion of mobile species, such as lithium ions, encounters periodic BN points offered by immobile framework species. These points deﬁne energetic barriers that separate two local minima,typicallyrepresentedby crystallographic sites for the ions. The energy barrier, also known as migration energy (Em), greatly inﬂuences ionic conductivity within the solid. Lower migration energies correspond to higher ionic mobility and conductivity. Understanding these differences is essential for designing and optimizing solid-state conductors for various applications. The diffusion process is examined by calculating mean square dis- placement (MSD). In a real system, the local energy landscape usually determines the hop of mobile ions. Major classes of fast ion conductors The translationally immobile framework anion plays a huge role in cationic conduction. Therefore, we classiﬁed the fast ion conductors based on their framework structures: layered oxide materials, polyhedral connecting fra- mework materials, and cluster anion-type materials. Each class is unique, and they have a distinct role in cation conduction. Layered oxide materials Layered oxide materials are a class of solid fast ion conductors that have a distinctive structure consisting of mobile cations sandwiched between rigid frameworklayers.Thesematerialsexhibithighionicconductivity,especially for alkali metal ions, and have potential applications in electrochemical devices. Two importantsub-classesoflayeredoxide materialsareβ-alumina and honeycomb layered oxide. β-alumina. In the middle of thetwentieth century, a remarkable scientiﬁc advancement emerged in the ﬁeld of SFICs with the groundbreaking discovery of β-alumina by Yao and Kummer30. One of the most striking features of β-alumina is its impressive Ag+ ion conductivity (3.5 × 10−2 S cm−166 at 25 ∘C), which rivals conventional liquid electro- lytes. This level of conductivity is exceptional and has attracted signiﬁcant attention from researchers in the ﬁeld of solid-state ionics. Notably, β- alumina also demonstrates fast ion conduction for divalent and even trivalent cation67. This characteristic expands its potential applications and highlights its versatility as a solid-state ionic conductor. The ability of β-alumina to facilitate the rapid conduction of alkali metal ions is attributed to its unique crystal structure. This structure comprises interconnected channels or tunnels that enable the efﬁcient movement of ions, enhancing their conductivity. Since the discovery of β-alumina, extensive experimental68–71 and theoretical67,72–75 research efforts have been dedicated to gaining deeper insights into its ion transport properties and stability. Moreover, synthe- sizing these materials is straightforward, allowing researchers to obtain high-quality samples for study and characterization. The general formula of β-alumina is M2O.xAl2O3 (where M = Li, Na, Ag, K, and Rb)30. This materialconsistsoftwodistinctsubgroups:β0 andβ″,eachcharacterizedbya unique structure (Fig. 3a, e). The β″ type exhibits higher ionic conductivity due to its distinctive framework structure, accommodating a larger number of vacant cationic sites. The crystal structure of β-alumina comprises compact layers of spinel blocks formed by Al3+ tetrahedra and octahedra coordinated with oxygens. These spinel blocks are sandwiched between mobile cations, with oxygen bridges connecting them to form a 3D hex- agonal structure. In the case of β0-alumina, the space group is P63/mcm, while for β″-alumina, it is R3m. The layer between the rigid spinel blocks is often called the conduction layer (Fig. 3a, e). Within the conduction layer, three different cationic sites exist: anti-Beevers-Ross (aBR), Beevers-Ross (BR), and mid-Oxygen (mO) (Fig. 3d)68. The sites are different based on the local oxygen environment, such as BR is formed by three top and three bottom oxygens, and aBR is formed by two oxygens (one top and one bottom).Thesesitesare crucialinfacilitatingcationicdiffusionand hopping within the material, as presented in Fig. 3b. Occupancy at these sites and the diffusion mechanism have been subjects of intense debate and investigation76–78. Kummer conducted systematic experimental studies on various monovalent counterparts (Li+, Na+, Ag+, K+, Rb+) of β-alumina79. The studies revealed that the ionic radius, particularly between Na+ and Ag+, was suitable for ion diffusion within the β-alumina framework (Fig. 3c). This observation suggests the existence of an optimal cation size that maximizes diffusion within the material. MD studies by Wolf, Walker, and Catlow80 provided structural and dynamical properties of β″-alumina using inter-atomic potential parameters suggested by Walker and Catlow81. These MD simulations revealed the importance of non-stoichiometric composition in enhancing cationic dif- fusion and observed a transition from low-temperature hopping transport to a higher-temperature liquid-like transport80. Further MD studies by Thomas and Zendejas82 focused on Na-β″-alumina and provided additional atomistic insights into the diffusion of Na+ ions, including correlation effects and the presence of mobile and immobile Na+ ions in the diffusion mechanism. The conduction mechanisms in β0-alumina and β″-alumina differ. In β0-alumina, the dominant conduction mechanism involves the migration of oxygen ions (O2−) through the crystal lattice, utilizing oxygen vacancies as diffusion paths. In β″-alumina, the conduction mechanism revolves around the migration of sodium ions (Na+) through the crystal lattice, facilitated by https://doi.org/10.1038/s43246-024-00550-z Review article Communications Materials | (2024) 5:122

the presence of oxygen vacancies. In addition tothe oxygen, repulsive forces between Na ions were found to play a crucial role in reducing the activation energy required for ion diffusion, as observed by Sato and Kikuchi83 and further emphasized by Wang and Pickett84. Accurate description of lattice vibration was executed by ref. 85. They developedasetofpotentialparametersbyﬁttingphononvibrationalmodes, providing a accurate representation of lattice vibrations in Ag β-alumina. Their studies showed that mobile Ag+ ions in the conducting plane are distributed over BR and aBR sites, exhibiting asymmetric large thermal amplitudes. The repulsion between Ag ions inﬂuences the dynamics, transitioning the diffusion mechanism from random hopping to coopera- tive motion. Honeycomb layered oxides. Honeycomb Layered oxide solids have attracted considerable attention as potential electrode for sodium-ion batteries since NaxCoO2 was ﬁrst introduced as a cathode material86. However, the cation diffusion mechanism is similar to the other elec- trolytes. Typical layered honeycomb oxides consist of alkali or coinage metal atoms sandwiched between slabs made exclusively of transition metal and chalcogen (or pnictogen) atoms arranged in edge-shared octahedra in a honeycomb fashion (Fig. 3f). These materials offer several advantages, such as wider interstitial spaces between two-dimensional polyhedral framework layers that facilitate cation migration, enabling high ionic conductivity at RT, and excellent chemical and ambient stability87. Meanwhile, a rigid octahedral framework layer completely hinders diffusion along the crystalline c-direction. The materials are classiﬁed based on the local cationic environment, with oxygen (tetra- hedral, octahedral, or prismatic) sharing rectangular faces, thereby creating a wide BN for facile cation transport88. These layered honeycomb oxide structures differ from the β-alumina structure, where oxygen atoms are located in the conduction layer. Van der Waals forces weakly connect the framework layers in these honeycomb oxides, and the inter-layer distance can be adjusted by framework modiﬁcations or a larger size cationic substitution. Alkali ion conductivity is signiﬁcantly inﬂuenced by the inter-slab distance, cationic concentration, and their different octahedral arrangements in the framework layer. Several experimental and theoretical studies, including MD simula- tions and topological analysis, have been conducted to gain insights into alkaline ion conduction and material stability mechanisms88–90. Evstigneeva et al. synthesized a series of honeycomb layered materials, Na2M2TeO6 (where M = Ni, Zn, Mg, and Co), and discovered surprisingly high ionic conductivity88. The materials containing nickel (Ni) are well-suited for utilization as cathode materials, whereas materials substituted with zinc (Zn) and magnesium (Mg), offering a low electronic conductivity, are particularly suitable for serving as electrolytes, demonstrating noteworthy Na+ ion conductivities of 5.7 × 10−4 S cm−1 and 2.3 × 10−4 S cm−1 at RT, respectively91,92. Further investigations, focusing on the impact of homo- valent calcium ion (Ca2+) substitution and heterovalent gallium ion (Ga3+) substitution at the zinc (Zn) site within the Na2Zn2TeO6 structure, unveiled augmented ionic conductivities, measuring 7.5 × 10−4 S cm−1 and 1.1 × 10−3 S cm−1 at RT, respectively93,94. These ﬁndings indicate a pro- gression towards the superionic regime, deﬁned by ionic conductivities exceeding 1.0 × 10−3 S cm−1. Despite several improvements in materials synthesis, the funda- mental understanding was lacking. Taking a broader perspective, MD simulations of Na2Ni2TeO6 aim to understand the mechanism of sodium ion transport in honeycomb layered oxide materials. Sau and Kumar89 proposed interatomic potential for performing force-ﬁeld-based MD simulations on the series of honeycomb layered oxides (Na2M2TeO6). The force ﬁeld accurately reproduced the structural and dynamical properties observed experimentally. The MD studies revealed detailed cationic diffusion pathways, energy barriers along the diffusion path (Fig. 3f), and cationic migration mechanisms. The crystal structure of Na2Ni2TeO6 consists of three distinct cationic sites: 6g, 4c, and 2a, which are located at the center of trigonal bi-prisms formed by face- or edge- sharing NiO6 or TeO6 octahedra. The 2a site is energetically less favor- able due to the strong electrostatic repulsion between the Na+ ion and the Te6+ ion in the adjacent TeO6 octahedra. MD simulations revealed that the Na+ ions preferentially occupy the 6g and 4c sites, in agreement with the experimental ﬁndings of ref. 95. The 2a site becomes accessible only at temperatures above 500 K, but no phase transition has been reported at such high temperatures. The MD simulations also indicated that the 4c site is the most stable site for the Na+ ions; the number of 4c sites is equal to the number of Na+ ions, implying that some Na+ ions have to occupy the slightly higher energy 6g sites for avoiding a strongly correlated diffusion. Therefore, the most probable diffusion pathway for the Na+ ions is 4c-6g-4c89. The presence of Na+ ions in the higher energy sites suggests a cooperative mechanism of Na+ ion migration. The conductivity can be tuned by varying the cationic concentrations among the inter-layer on the conduction layer, as shown in Fig. 3g96, where there is a scope for studying concerted motion and their role in hopping energy barrier. A general characteristic of honeycomb layered material can be deﬁned in a radar plot, as shown in Fig. 3h. Sau et al. expanded their MD study to several other honeycomb layered oxide materials, such as A2Ni2TeO6 97, where A = Li, Na, and K, and Na2LiFeTeO6 98. Figure 3j indicates the goodness of the structural ﬁtting with the XRD structure, whereas a comparative study in A2Ni2TeO6 for different cation sizes can provide insights into how different factors, such as ion–ion repulsion99, pressure, temperature, and structural stability, affect the diffusion, con- ductivity, and occupancy of cations at different cationic sites. The study revealed an exponential relationship between cationic diffusion, inter-layer distances (Fig. 3k), inverse relationship with activation energy (Fig. 3l), and different cationic occupancy patterns with increasing cationic sizes63. Notably, a ring-type diffusion mechanism was found in Na2LiFeTeO6, similar to other classes of materials like garnet100. This ring-type diffusion is also known as a billiard-ball mechanism101. Later, Masese et al. made signiﬁcant contributions to the domain of high-voltage battery applications by identifying and reporting several pro- mising materials102,103. Conventionally, materials in this category are char- acterized by a single conduction layer. However, their work has yielded a particularly intriguing material, namely Ag6M2TeO6 (where M can repre- sent Ni, Mg, or other transition metal atoms), which exhibits a distinctive structure featuring bi-layers of Ag atoms within Ag-rich crystalline domains, as depicted in Fig. 3i90. This bi-layer-type honeycomb layered oxide conﬁguration represents a unique and novel structural motif. In order to explore the distinctive properties of these bilayer-type honeycomb layered oxides, a preliminary MD simulation was conducted using a previously reported force ﬁeld, with interaction parameters similar to those of Na2Ni2TeO6. During this simulation, the polyhedral layers were held ﬁxed at their centers to prevent any bending. Interestingly, the theo- retical simulation successfully conﬁrmed the formation of these bilayer structures using the predeﬁned force ﬁeld. In the case of Ag6M2TeO6, it was observed that the inter-layer distance is relatively substantial, approximately 6 Å, in contrast to Na2Ni2TeO6, which exhibits an inter-layer distance of approximately 3 Å. Consequently, mobile cations within the bilayer tend to approach the oxygen layer, resulting in a splitting of the Ag+ conduction layer. However, it is essential to emphasize that a more comprehensive and detailed investigation is needed to gain a thorough understanding of the cationicdiffusionalpathwaysand theunderlyingdiffusionmechanismsthat govern these intriguing materials. Key challenges and prospects. Polyhedral connecting framework materials Polyhedral Connecting Framework Materials is another class that exhibits a 3D network of polyhedra. These polyhedra, which can be of various shapes, such as tetrahedra and octahedra, are connected at their corners or edges to form a continuous framework. This structure creates channels or cages where mobile ions can reside. The connectivity and geometry of the poly- hedra can greatly inﬂuence the material’s properties, including its thermal stability, electronic structure, and ion conductivity. Whereas, higher ionic conductivity has been achieved for Li-rich, “stuffed garnets,” such as Li5La3M2O12 (M = Nb, Ta, and Sb), Li6ALa2M2O12 (A = Mg, Ca, Sr, and Ba; M = Nb and Ta), and Li7La3M2O12 (M = Zr and Sn)106 where Li ions occupy the tetrahedral as well as octahedral interstitial sites partially, increasing migrational entropy, ΔSm (Eq. One of the most widely studied compositions of the lithium garnet series is Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO). This high-conducting cubic garnet was reported by ref. 104, and later on, the tetragonal phase was detected at a lower temperature by ref. 107. The cubic phase exhibits two orders of magnitude higher conductivity than the tetragonal phase108. Several com- putational studies have been conducted to explain such behavior109,110. The low-temperature tetragonal phase exhibits synchronous collective Li+ ion hopping, causing a high activation energy barrier. In cubic LLZO, the Li+ ﬁnds unoccupied sites, resulting in uncorrelated Li+ motion that costs less activation energy100. In contrast, a few ab initio MD studies by refs. 111,45 identiﬁed the concerted motion of Li+ ions (two or three Li+ ions jump together). Therefore, the Li+ ion diffusion mechanism is still under debate. Hu et al.112, and others113–115 reported that higher valent ion (Al3+) sub- stitution at Li sublattice improves the stability of cubic garnet of nominal composition in Li7La3Zr2O12. The Al3+ substitution generates more Li sites, leading to higher conﬁgurational entropy and reducing the free energy barrier between two Li+ ion hops. Furthermore, the aliovalent substitutions (e.g., Ta5+) at Zr sites also enhance the ionic conductivity116,117. An order of magnitude conductivity is enhanced from Li5La3Ta2O12 to Li6BaLa2Ta2O12 116,118,119 where the Li ions are occupied in tetrahedral as well as octahedral sites118,120. In 2011, ref. 6 reported a unique 3D framework structure (Li10GeP2S12) known as an LGPS-type structure, which exhibited a remarkable order of magnitude higher lithium-ion conductivity (12 mS cm−1 at ambient temperature) than the best Li+ ion conductivity reported in last decades among the sulﬁdes. This discovery represented a signiﬁcant breakthrough in solid-state fast ion conductors and prompted further exploration of these materials for application in ASSBs. The LGPS-type material has a general formula of Li4−xGe1−xPxS4, where x = 2/3. The crystal structure can be described as a tetragonal cell with space group P42/nmc. The framework structure consists of (Ge0.5P0.5)S4, PS4, and LiS4-tetrahedra, forming a complex network. The (Ge0.5P0.5)S4 tetrahedra and LiS6 octahedra are connected by edge-sharing, forming a one-dimensional (1D) chain along the c-direction, further inter- connected by PS4 tetrahedra. The lithium-ion channel comprises 16h, 4d, 4c, and 8f sites, although the existence of the 4c site remains a subject of debate. The origin of the high ionic conduction exhibited by LGPS-type materials has been extensively investigated through theoretical studies. MD simulations suggest that the high conductivity may arise from col- lective ion migrations along the 1D path facilitated by Coulombic interactions among the lithium ions. This phenomenon, known as the cooperative migration mechanism, involves the coordination and movement of multiple Li+ ions within the available conduction pathways, resulting in enhanced ionic conductivity. Even though LGPS-type structures exhibit high Li+ ion conductivity, a portion of Li+ ions remains localized at octahedral sites, not contributing to Li+ ion diffusion. This material exhibits highly anisotropic Li+ conduction through partially occupied tetrahedral Li-sites with a low activation energy of 0.24 eV. However, the atomic origins of these characteristics remained unclear until Mo et al. shed light on the topic by conducting ab initio MD simulations, supporting the hypothesis of Li+ ion diffusion along the c- direction59. Adams and Rao109 performed MD simulations based on force ﬁelds to gain deeper insights, revealing the atomistic dynamics of Li ions. They found that Li+ ions are distributed along the c-direction among several interstitial Li sites. The study also indicated the possibility of PS4 3/GeS4 2− rotation, which facilitates Li+ ion dynamics through a paddle-wheel mechanism121. To replace the expensive germanium (Ge) component, ref.122synthesized Li10SnP2S12,which gained considerable attentiondue to its comparable ionic conductivity to liquids or polymers, negligible elec- tronic conductivity, and cost-effectiveness. A recently developed material, Li11Si2PS12 (LGPS-type material) by ref. 123, exhibited higher conductivity than LGPS at RT with an activation energy of ~0.19 eV. Subsequently, ref. 2 synthesized materials such as Li9.54Si1.74P1.44S11.7Cl0.3 with an ionic con- ductivity of 25 mS cm−1 at RT, posing a similar structure as LGPS. Another study by ref. 124 investigated Na11Sn2PnX12 (Pn = P, Sb; X = S, Se) and found that framework tetrahedral rotation (PnX3 4 ) introduced dynamic frustration in the energy landscape of Na11Sn2PS12 and Na11Sn2PSe12, enabling facile sodium (Na) ion diffusion. For a conductivity comparison, an Arrhenius plot is displayed in Fig. 4f. In SFICs, introducing halogen is pivotal in transforming the ion dif- fusion mechanism from 1D to 3D at ambient temperature. This phenom- enon is attributed to the ability of halogens to diminish the interaction between the framework anion and the migrating ions, thereby facilitating facile ion transport. In the silicon-based system, Li9.54Si1.74P1.44S11.7Cl0.3 crystal structure exempliﬁes the transformative effect of halogen incor- poration. As depicted in Fig. 4d, the unit cell comprises 1D polyhedral chains interconnected by PX4 (X = Cl, Br, I) tetrahedra, providing a network of interconnected pathways (Fig. 4e) for Li+ ion migration. The Li+ ions occupy the 16h, 8f, and 4c interstitial sites. Thio-/LISICONs. Signiﬁcant research efforts have been dedicated to enhancing the ionic conductivity in Lithium Super Ionic Conductors (LISICONs). In 1978, Hong identiﬁed poor ionic conductivity (10−7 S cm−1 at ambient temperature) in Li14Zn(GeO4)4 and related materials such as Li4GeO4-LiVO4, Li2+2xZn1−xGeO4, Li2O-V2O5-SiO2, and Li4SiO4-Li3PO4, which were synthesized around the same period and exhibited slightly improved ionic conductivity125–129. Replacing oxide ions (O2−) with sulﬁde ions (S2−) in the LISICON structure has signiﬁcantly enhanced cationic conductivity. This phenomenon can be attributed to the larger ionic radius and lower electronegativity of S2−compared to O2−, both of which favor high ionic conductivity. The general formula for thio- LISICONs is Li4xM1yM0 yS4S4, where M can be Si, Ge, or Sn; M0 can be P, Al, Zn, Ga, or Sb; and x and y are compositional parameters. Notable materials in this class include Li4GeS4, Li4SiS4, Li4SnS4, Li3PS4, and Li2ZrS3), and Li2ZrS3,all of which exhibit ionic conductivities in theorder of 10−5 S cm−1. The structural arrangement of thio-LISICONs differs from that of LGPS-type materials. In thio-LISICONs, Li+ ions and Ge atoms are located at the octahedral and tetrahedral sites, respectively, and S2−are arranged in a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) fashion (Fig. 4(g)), whereas in LGPS-type materials, the S2−are arranged in a body-centered cubic (bcc) position. Aliovalent doping can further enhance the Li+ ion conductivity of thio-LISICONs. For instance, in the case of homovalent substitutions in Li3PO4, replacing O with S reduces the activation energy for Li+ ion migration from 1.5 to 0.5 eV. NASICON exhibits promising characteristics, including high 3D ionic conductivity, low thermal expansion, as well as high chemical stability. Complex hydrides. In SFIC, the comparison between β-alumina and NASICONs has been a subject of scientiﬁc exploration. However, it was not until 2007 that hydride materials, which have been studied for hydrogen storage, were recognized for their potential as fast ion conductors156. A pivotal discovery was made when it was found that Li+ ions exhibited signiﬁcant conduction behavior in LiBH4 after a structural transition from orthorhombic to hexagonal at 380 K with an approximate conductivity of 10−3 S cm−1157–159. This breakthrough propelled the research focus towards hydrides and their derivatives as solid electrolytes for ASSBs, owing to their remarkable ionic conductivity, high thermal and chemical stability, lightweight nature, stability against metal anode, and favorable mechanical properties, making them an ideal interface between the electrode and electrolyte. In light of the promising characteristics exhibited by hydrides, it is imperative to address several formidable challenges before realizing their practical utility, with a notable concern being their relatively deﬁcient ionic conductivity at RT157. Taking lithium borohydride (LiBH4) as an illustrative example, it is evident that its RT ionic conductivity is signiﬁcantly limited, being three to four orders of magnitude lower than desired157. However, a phase transition occurs at elevated temperatures, speciﬁcally at 388 K, leading to a remarkable augmentation in lithium-ion mobility, culminating in an impressive conductivity value of 5 × 10−3 S cm−1 at 423 K156,158–160. This underscores the pivotal role played by phase transitions within this class of materials. Consequently, it is paramount to gain a comprehensive under- standing of the intricacies surrounding phase transition phenomena, encompassing the underlying factors and origins. This improved ionic conductivity in LiBH4 arises due to the rotational disorder of the [BH4]−units in the high-T phase, a unique characteristic of such materials. The cationic sites’ lattice disorder contributes to the high ionic conductivity, and the rotational disorder of BH4 units has been investigated through techniques such as synchrotron X-ray powder dif- fraction, QENS, and ab initio MD simulations161–164.
