In pursuit of developing efﬁcient solid electrolytes for advanced battery technologies, signiﬁcant research has been dedi- cated to thiophosphate-based materials. Among these, lithium argyr- odites have emerged as a highly researched class, with promising ionic conductive properties reaching up to 24 mS cm−1182. However, it is important to note that these materials often exhibit varying degrees of disorder, particularly in the form of anion exchange between halogens and sulfur sites. This anion exchange has a signiﬁcant inﬂuence on the cationic transport properties, prompting numerous studies aimed at understanding the impact of iso- and aliovalent substitutions on this exchange process. Nevertheless, altering the chemical composition introduces complexities in comprehending the resultant transport properties, thereby making it challenging to isolate individual inﬂuences. Arising from the general formula Li7PS6, argyrodites display a transi- tion from a normal to a superionic phase (orthorhombic to a cubic phase, featuring the space group F43m). Their RT ionic conductivity remains relativelylow, with valuesaround 1.6 × 10−6 S cm−1183. The high-conducting phase canbe stabilized byintroducingcompositionssuch asLi6PS5X (where X represents a halogen atom like Cl, Br, I, or a vacancy). In the cubic phase, Li+ ions occupy 24g and 48h sites, S atoms are found in 4a and 4c sites, P atoms are situated in 4b sites, and either halide atoms (X) or vacancies occupy 4a sites. Speciﬁcally, the S atoms at 4a sites form PS4 tetrahedra with P atoms at 4b sites, while the S atoms at 4c sites bridge between PS4 tetra- hedra (as depicted in Fig. 7a)184–188. The Li ions are distributed in octahedral coordination around the S atoms. The presence of various interstitial sites surrounding the halide ions facilitates high ionic conductivity (Fig. 7c), typically within the range of 10−2–10−3 S cm−1 at RT, with low activation energies typically around 0.2 to 0.3 eV189. Among the single halide argyrodites, Li6PS5Cl exhibits the highest ionic conductivity at ambient temperature, ~10−3 S cm−1, followed by Li6PS5Br with around 10−4 S cm−1, while Li6PS5I displays the lowest ionic conductivity, ~10−6 S cm−1, as illustrated in Fig. 7b. The origin of such high ionic conductivity in Li6PS5Cl and Li6PS5Br has been the focus of several investigations. It has been observed that disorder involving S2−/X−site occupancy plays a signiﬁcant role, resulting in ionic conductivity that is three ordersof magnitude lower infully ordered Li6PS5I. On the other hand, ref. 190 argued that an increase in Li-ion concentration and Li-site disorder is the primary contributing factor. A comprehensive investigation into bulk conductivity within the argyrodite material Li6PS5Cl was conducted, employing a combination of 7Li nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) experiments and DFT-based MD simulations by ref. 191. This study found two distinct lithium-ion diffusion mechanisms within this material: (1) Local hops: The study revealed that Li+-ions within Li6PS5Cl undergo local hops within the cage-like structures formedbytheirpositionsaroundthesulfur(S)orchlorine(Cl)atoms.These local hops represent a crucial aspect of Li+-ion conductivity within the material. (2) Inter-Cage hops: In addition to the local hops, the study identiﬁed inter-cage hops as a Li+-ion diffusion within the crystalline bulk structure of Li6PS5Cl. This implies that the movement of Li+-ions between different cage-like structures is a critical factor inﬂuencing the overall lithium-ion conductivity in this material. Notably, ref.192 put forth an alternative perspective, offering new insights into the diffusion mechanisms within argyrodite materials, espe- cially in cases whereX represents Cl, Br, or I. Their investigation employed 31P magic angle spinning NMR to probe the rotation of the PS4 3 units within these materials, yielding the following observations: In cases where X corresponds to Cl or Br, they detected a coupling between the rotation of PS4 3 units and the diffusion of lithium ions, as illustrated in Fig. 7d. This coupling promotes inter-cage jumps of lithium ions, facilitating long-range diffusion within the material. However, in the instance where X represents I, they noted that, despite the presence of local lithium-ion motion, lithium ions do not exhibit long-range inter-cage hop. This is attributed to the decoupling of PS4 3 unit from lithium-ion diffusion, primarily due to the soft lattice nature of the material. Additionally, various aliovalent substitutions have been explored to enhance ionic conductivity195,196. These materials encounter challenges such as low ionic conductivity at RT and high sensitivity to ambient conditions. The substantial anionic rotational disorder represents a formidable barrier to gaining structural insights during the high- conductivity phase. Elucidating the intricacies of structure-property relationships and comprehending the impact of anion exchange and substitution on ion transport mechanisms within cluster anion-type materials necessitates the application of sophisticated experimental and theoretical methodologies. However, anion rotation is a key feature for designing high-conducting materials. General understanding and common features The development of solid ion conductors has primarily relied on the ion conduction mechanism described by Eq. (6), where ion movement occurs through hopping within a crystalline lattice11,211. Many structural families have demonstrated reasonably high Li-ion conductivity at RT, with the ability to vary Li-ion conductivity by several orders of magnitude within the same crystal framework structures10,211. Therefore, this section is dedicated to understanding the common and unique characteristics of the fast ion- conducting materials examined in this review. Coordination number Early studies found that the conditions in which the high ionic conductivity is realized with monovalent cation in a four- (tetrahedral) and three- coordinated conﬁgurations with the anions212. Recent studies have expan- ded this idea to link the high ionic conductivity observed in lithium sulﬁdes (e.g., LGPS and Li7P3S11) to bcc sulfur-sublattice, which can lead to energetically-equivalent tetrahedral (four-coordinated) sites of lithium and large transport channels11. Collective motion Several studies revealed that the collective (or cooperative) transport of lithium ions can ﬂatten the migration energy barrier, thereby facilitating rapid ion conduction in materials like LGPS, cubic LLZO, and NASICONs152,213,214.Inthesematerials,ithasbeenobserved that,onaverage, two to three Li-ions migrate simultaneously45,111,215. For instance, Burbano et al.100 identiﬁed the presence of string-like ion clusters that engage in cooperative motion within LLZO.Similarly, a ring-like mechanism was also reported in Na2LiFeTeO6 98. On the contrary, some studies reported that the strong cation-cation correlation is responsible for slow cation diffusion100. Hence, lower activation energy due to the collective diffusion of ions is subject to further investigation. Paddle-wheel effect Most recently, superionic conductors (such as Li3PS4, Li2B12H12, NaCB9H10, LiNaSO4, Na2SO4, Na3PO4, LiBH4, Li3SBF4, Na3SBCl4, etc.) containing anion clusters (i.e., PS4 3−, B12H12 2−, CB9H10 −, SO4 2−, PO4 3−, BH4 −, BF4 −, BCl4 −, etc.) have become a fertile group to search for high ionic conductivity175,177,180,216,217. An interesting feature of these ionic conductors is the so-called paddle-wheel effect characterized by a strong correlation between the translational motion of the cation and the rotational motion of anion cluster216, as depicted in Fig. 8(c), where the anionic rotation triggers the cationic diffusion. Under thermal excitation, non-spherical clusters can lead to a rotationally disordered phase, creating low-energy pathways for ionic migrations and greatly enhancing ionic conductivity175,217–219. This is exempliﬁed by the high Na-ion conductivity of 30 mS cm−1 of NaCB9H10 as it enters a rotationally disordered phase at RT. Kweon et al.175 supported the paddle-wheel behavior in A2B12H12 (A = Li and Na) by overlapping the translational diffusion frequency of cation and rotational frequency of anion. Therefore, fully exploiting the rotational degrees of freedom and utilizing the paddle-wheel effect could be a viable way to achieve high cation conductions. Most of the known cluster-containing ionic conductors exhibit a transition to the rotational disordered phase at high temperatures (higher than RT)167,172,220. It has been found that an amorphous structure with low density and a relatively large volume to accommodate the cluster cansupportthepaddle-wheeleffectevenatlowtemperatures(e.g.,RT)216,221. Despite the inﬂuence of polyanion rotation on cationic conduction, there is a lack of direct evidence, which makes this a controversial phenomenon. Such as in the case of Li2SO4, and α-Na3PO4 222, the polyanion rotation unexpectedly reduces the cationic conduction. On the other hand, ref. 223 argued that the doping of BH4 in Li-argyrodite enhanced the Li+-ion con- duction, which originated from weak interaction between Li and BH4 instead of the anion rotational effect. Therefore, the high cationic conduc- tion driven by the anion rotational effect is under a long debate. Introducing anharmonicity Anharmonicity is the deviation of a system from being a harmonic oscil- lator, which means that the restoring force is not proportional to the dis- placement of the system (Fig. 8f). Anharmonicity plays an important role in ion conduction. Several theoretical and experimental studies (DFT calcu- lations and neutron scattering experiments) have been performed recently to understand the phonon modes that are coupled most strongly with ionic conductivity and assess the role of anharmonicity. It has been ascertained that the anharmonicity inherent in the phonon vibrational modes of the host lattice exhibits substantial coupling with cationic diffusion. This phe- nomenon has been notably observed in AgI224. The recognized strong coupling between mobile ions and the host lattice holds pivotal importance for the diffusion process. Furthermore, investigations extended to materials like AgCrSe2, CuCrSe2, Li7P3S11, Li10GeP2S12, β-Li3PS4, Li3YBr6, and Li3ErCl6 have revealed analogous coupling phenomena (refs. 225,226). Structures that possess 3D diffusion pathways11 often exhibit a correlation with high ion conductivity, while lower dimensionalities227 often result in reduced ionic transport due to the potential obstruction of diffusion channels by defects228, even though the conductivity eq. (6) tells a different story, as the dimension term is in the denominator. Optimal bottleneck radius Ionic conductors with intrinsically low activation barriers are highly desirable. SFICs exhibit ionic conduction through polyhedral faces, leading to dynamic changes in the coordination environment of the migrating ion. These transitions create structural bottlenecks (BNs) within the diffusion pathway, directly inﬂuencing the activation energy barriers associated with ion migration229. Edge-sharing polyhedra typically present less favorable pathways for ion transport compared to face-sharing conﬁgurations. This is attributed to the generally smaller BNs, which encountered signiﬁcant changes in the coordination environment during ion jumps in edge-sharing structures230. Structural modiﬁcations arising from substitutions can frus- trate energy landscapes175,231,232, which impacts changing BNs radius233,234 (see Fig. 2a), consequently changing of the migration mechanism11,111. https://doi.org/10.1038/s43246-024-00550-z Review article Communications Materials | (2024) 5:122

Generally, substituting larger atoms into the polyhedral framework struc- ture results in a decrease in the activation barrier (see Fig. 5d) due to a widening of the diffusion bottleneck11,139). Of particular importance are materials possessing a percolating, 3D extended network composed of connected polyhedra with similar coordi- nation environments (widening BN radius). This structural characteristic can be achieved, for instance, by exclusively incorporating face-sharing polyhedra of the mobile species11. Such an arrangement minimizes the change in the coordination environment and naturally results in low acti- vation barriers. However, it is crucial to recognize that an excessively wide BN does not necessarily guarantee enhanced ion conduction134. In many cases, an optimal, moderate BN size proves efﬁcient ion transport, con- tingent upon the speciﬁc cation sizes and framework anion characteristics. Na-designing principles While Li-ion and Na-ion conductors share similar chemistry, their optimal design principles differ. Unlike Li-ion conductors, Na-ion conductors beneﬁt from face-sharing high-coordination number (CN) sites in their diffusion channels. This unique feature, proposed by ref. 46, is exempliﬁed by Na β-alumina and P2-type NaCoO2. Both materials possess face-sharing prismatic Na sites with large bottleneck sizes, enabling direct Na+ hopping with low energy barriers (0.26 eV in P2-type NaCoO2). This contrasts with structures lacking face-sharing, like O3-type NaMO2, which exhibit high energy barriers (0.76 eV) due to unfavorable intermediate sites. The face- sharing arrangement facilitates efﬁcient Na+ movement by avoiding these energy-intensive pathways. Therefore, in designing high-performance Na- ion conductors, incorporating face-sharing high-CN sites emerges as a critical strategy. Conclusions
and future directions

In conclusion, we focused on the major classes of fast ion conductors, such as layered oxides, polyhedral connecting frameworks, and cluster anion-type materials, and a comprehensive exploration of their frame- work structure on ion conduction mechanisms, and strategies for enhancing ionic conductivity have been undertaken. The pivotal roles played by experimental and theoretical approaches in unraveling the atomistic insights of these materials have been highlighted. Our analysis revealed that fast ion conduction is a complex phenomenon that depends on various factors, such as structural bottlenecks, framework con- nectivity, carrier concentration, anion rotation, cation-cation correlation etc. Furthermore, mono-valent and di-valent cations need different structural features for fast ion conduction. Based on a systematic understanding of these factors, we suggest general principles and guidelines for designing and optimizing fast ion conductors. Future research in solid-state ion conductors should explore avenues that enhance ion mobility beyond the current limitations. Three promising strategies include: Harnessing anion rotation and neutral molecule incorporation Materials exhibiting anion rotation and integrating neutral molecules offer signiﬁcant potential for achieving exceptional ionic conductivity. This is particularly impactful for materials already possessing good ionic con- ductivity, potentially pushing their performance to new heights. Alloying two different materials The successful implementation of combining distinct closo-type complex hydrides exempliﬁes the efﬁcacy of this approach and encourages its application to other classes of materials. Alloying offers a unique pathway to tailor material properties by leveraging the synergistic effects between dif- ferent components. This can lead to novel materials with enhanced ionic conductivity, surpassing the limitations of individual constituents. For instance, alloying can optimize the energy landscape for ion migration. By carefully selecting and combining materials with complementary ionic conductivities and activation energies, researchers can create pathways that facilitate smoother ion movement and reduce energy barriers. This strategy can also enhance structural stability, prevent phase transitions and decomposition that might hinder performance, and ﬁne-tune material composition through alloying, allowing for the optimization of other desirable characteristics, such as mechanical strength, thermal stability, and electrochemical window. Leveraging machine learning and high throughput screening While this review does not explore in detail the ML applications within fast ion conduction. encompassing monovalent to multivalent ion conductors and their key properties can signiﬁcantly accelerate materials research by facilitating understanding and screening of potential candidates48,60,252. These advanced computational tools can overcome the limitations of traditional methods, providing a more accurate and holistic understanding of ion diffusion and conductivity within complex material systems. Finally, it is essential to acknowledge that realizing solid-state fast ion conductors for all-solid-state battery applications necessitates con- sideration beyond high ionic conductivity. Other critical factors include wide electrochemical windows, minimal electronic conductivity, robust thermal and chemical stability, electrode compatibility, and environ- mental friendliness.
